title: Problem Overview
content: **Erdős Problem #283** connects Egyptian fractions (sums of distinct unit fractions like 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1) with additive representation by polynomial values. Given a polynomial p with positive leading coefficient and no universal divisor, can every large m be written as p(n₁) + ... + p(nₖ) where 1/n₁ + ... + 1/nₖ = 1? Graham (1963) proved it for p(x) = x. Alekseyev (2019) proved it for p(x) = x². The general case remains open.
mathContext: We use Polynomial for ℤ[X], Filter.atTop for 'sufficiently large' quantifiers, and Finset for finite sums. The polynomial evaluation p.eval n computes p(n). Egyptian fractions have ancient origins but continue to generate open problems in modern number theory.

title: Egyptian Fractions
content: **IsEgyptianDecomposition s** requires all elements positive and ∑ 1/n = 1 as rationals. Two examples are verified via native_decide: **{2,3,6}** (1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1) and **{2,4,6,12}** (1/2 + 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12 = 1). The Finset representation ensures elements are distinct.
mathContext: The ancient Egyptians used unit fractions exclusively. The condition ∑ 1/n = 1 is computed over ℚ to avoid rounding issues. The examples are verified by native_decide which checks the rational arithmetic at compile time.

title: Polynomial Condition and Main Conjecture
content: **HasNoUniversalDivisor** ensures no d ≥ 2 divides all p(n). **X_has_no_universal_divisor** (proved): if d | p(1) = 1 then d is a unit, contradicting d ≥ 2. **sq_has_no_universal_divisor** (proved): same argument via p(1) = 1² = 1. **ErdosCondition p** asks: for sufficiently large m, ∃ Egyptian decomposition s with ∑ p(n) = m. **erdos_283_conjecture**: does this hold for all polynomials?
mathContext: The proofs use isUnit_of_dvd_one and Int.isUnit_iff to show d | 1 forces d ∈ {±1}. The ErdosCondition uses Filter.atTop to express 'for all sufficiently large m'. The conjecture quantifies over all ℤ[X], making it very general.

title: Graham and Alekseyev Theorems
content: **graham_theorem** (axiom): ErdosCondition X holds — every large m is a sum n₁ + ... + nₖ where 1/n₁ + ... + 1/nₖ = 1. **alekseyev_theorem** (axiom): for m > 8542, same with squares n₁² + ... + nₖ². **alekseyev_example** (proved via native_decide): ∑ n² over {2,4,6,12} = 200.
mathContext: Graham's 1963 proof appeared in J. Austral. Math. Soc. and uses detailed combinatorial constructions. Alekseyev's 2019 result gives the explicit threshold 8542. The verified example 2²+4²+6²+12² = 200 provides a concrete witness.

title: Extensions and Structure
content: **van_doorn_linear/quadratic** (axioms): extensions to p(x) = x+c and p(x) = x²+c. **cassels_theorem** (axiom): without the Egyptian constraint, representation always works — highlighting how much harder the constraint makes the problem. **trivial_egyptian** (proved): {1} is a decomposition since 1/1 = 1. **infinitely_many_egyptian_decompositions** (axiom): the set of decompositions is infinite.
mathContext: Cassels (1960) resolved the unconstrained version, showing the Egyptian fraction requirement is the real source of difficulty. The trivial decomposition {1} is degenerate but illustrates the base case. Splitting 1/n into 1/(n+1) + 1/(n(n+1)) generates infinitely many decompositions.

title: Summary Theorem
content: **erdos_283_summary** packages both known results as a proved conjunction: (1) Graham's theorem for p(x) = x, and (2) Alekseyev's theorem for p(x) = x² with threshold 8542. The proof is ⟨graham_theorem, alekseyev_theorem⟩.
mathContext: The two-part conjunction captures the partially solved status: two specific polynomial cases are resolved while the general conjecture remains open. Unlike fully solved Erdős problems, there is no single comprehensive result — the problem requires case-by-case analysis for each polynomial degree.
